about: One child-facing fact per BUILT species, for Joe's sign-off alongside the model, the collection and the name. Drafted, then independently fact-checked. Covers the 96 species in SHIPPED_SPECIES on 29 Jul 2026: the frozen base 24, plus garden (13), home-pets (14), woodland (16), africa (13) and farm (16). The species manager shipped farm, four cage birds and two woodland game birds while this file was being written, and those 22 were drafted and checked in a second pass. Species in a collection not listed in coveredCollections have no fact yet — see that field.
notCovered: Every other collection in the roster is unbuilt, so there is nothing to sign off. When the manager ships one, its members need adding here or they reach Joe's bench factless. The test asserts full coverage WITHIN coveredCollections only, so a newly shipped collection will not break anyone else's gate — which also means nothing shouts. Adding the collection id above turns the tripwire back on.
method: Each fact was drafted first, then handed to a separate checker told to REFUTE it rather than confirm it, using web search against zoos, museums, universities, wildlife trusts and government agencies. 'flagged' means the checker refuted the wording, found it contested, or could only reach a weak source. A flagged fact has NOT been quietly reworded to sound safe: the drafted wording is preserved in 'fact', and any defensible alternative the checker could source sits in 'proposedRewrite' for Joe to accept or ignore.
guardrails: Brief S19: UK English, bright, never scary. No predation, killing, death or frightening threat framing. Juno is six and learning to read, so one or two short sentences, plain words, one idea.

fields.check: verified | flagged — my checking, not Joe's.
fields.source: URL the checker actually read, supporting the fact as worded.
fields.sourceNote: What that source says, plus any caveat the checker raised.
fields.proposedRewrite: Only on flagged rows. A defensible alternative wording, sourced. Not applied.
fields.verdict: JOE'S. Leave blank until he rules.
fields.replacement: JOE'S. He may rewrite a fact rather than reject it.

facts.fact: Beavers build dams across streams with sticks and mud.
facts.sourceNote: NWF: beavers build dams across streams from branches and sticks packed with mud and gravel.

facts.fact: Bees dance to tell other bees where the flowers are.
facts.sourceNote: AMNH on the waggle dance (von Frisch): it communicates direction and distance to a food source to nestmates.

facts.fact: Rabbits can see nearly all the way around without turning their head.
facts.sourceNote: Eyes set on the sides of the head give close to 360-degree vision. There is a small blind spot right in front of the nose, which is why the fact says 'nearly' and not 'all the way'.

facts.fact: Cats sleep for much of the day, often more than twelve hours.
facts.sourceNote: Adult cats average 12-16 hours of sleep a day.

facts.fact: A caterpillar changes inside a chrysalis and comes out as a butterfly.
facts.sourceNote: AMNH: the caterpillar forms a chrysalis and reorganises inside it before emerging as a butterfly. Grown-up caveat only: it does not dissolve to 'total mush' as pop science often says, but the wording here does not claim that.

facts.fact: A chick uses a tiny egg tooth on its beak to tap its way out of the shell.
facts.sourceNote: Audubon: a temporary keratin egg tooth on the beak tip is used to pip the shell, and drops off after hatching.

facts.fact: Cows bring their food back up to chew it a second time.
facts.sourceNote: Britannica: cows regurgitate cud from the rumen back to the mouth to be chewed again.

facts.fact: Many crabs walk sideways because of the way their legs bend.
facts.sourceNote: Britannica: crab leg joints favour sideways movement. 'Many' rather than 'all' is deliberate — some crabs do move forwards.

facts.fact: Male deer grow new antlers every year and drop the old ones.
facts.sourceNote: US Fish and Wildlife Service: males shed antlers annually and regrow a new set each year.

facts.fact: A dog's sense of smell is far stronger than ours.
facts.sourceNote: University of Alaska Fairbanks. Published multipliers range from 1,000x to 100,000x depending on how it is measured, so the fact deliberately gives no number.

facts.fact: An elephant uses its trunk to drink, to wash, and to pick things up.
facts.sourceNote: San Diego Zoo: the trunk draws up water to drink and to spray for washing, and is dexterous enough to pick objects up.

facts.fact: Fish breathe underwater using gills instead of lungs.
facts.sourceNote: AMNH: fish take dissolved oxygen from water through gills. Lungfish and a few others are exceptions, but the general claim is standard.

facts.fact: A fox's bushy tail is called a brush, and it keeps the fox warm.
facts.sourceNote: RSPCA, in one sentence: foxes use their tails, 'also called a brush', for balance and warmth. An earlier Wildlife Trusts source supported only the name, so this was re-sourced.

facts.fact: A giraffe has seven bones in its neck, just like you do.
facts.sourceNote: San Diego Zoo: seven cervical vertebrae, the same count as a human, each one very much longer.

facts.fact: Wild boars love rolling in mud to keep cool.
facts.sourceNote: Wallowing in wild boar and other pigs is primarily about temperature — they have very few sweat glands and the mud cools by slow evaporation.

facts.fact: Koalas sleep for most of the day up in the gum trees.
facts.sourceNote: San Diego Zoo Global fact sheet: koalas spend roughly 19-20 hours a day resting or sleeping, and are arboreal.

facts.fact: Male lions grow a big furry mane around their head.
facts.sourceNote: San Diego Zoo: the mane starts growing around age one and fills in by about five. Caveat: males in some hot regions grow little or no mane, so this is typical rather than universal.

facts.fact: Most monkeys have a tail, but apes do not.
facts.sourceNote: Britannica: almost all monkeys have tails and apes do not. 'Most' covers tailless exceptions such as the Barbary macaque.

facts.fact: Pandas eat bamboo for most of the day.
facts.sourceNote: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance: giant pandas spend at least 12 hours a day eating bamboo.

facts.fact: Some parrots can copy sounds they hear, even people talking.
facts.sourceNote: Scientific American: parrots have a syrinx and neural pathways that let them mimic sounds including human speech.

facts.fact: Penguins cannot fly, but they swim beautifully with their flipper wings.
facts.sourceNote: Cornell Lab: no penguin flies; the wings evolved into stiff flippers that drive them through water.

facts.fact: Pigs roll in mud to keep cool, because they cannot sweat much.
facts.sourceNote: University of Missouri Extension: pigs have very few functional sweat glands and rely on wallowing to cool by evaporation.

facts.fact: A polar bear's fur looks white, but its skin underneath is black.
facts.sourceNote: Polar Bears International: the skin under the fur is black and the fur itself is translucent, not white. The reason WHY the skin is black is still a hypothesis, so the fact does not claim one.

facts.fact: Every tiger has its own pattern of stripes, and no two are the same.
facts.sourceNote: WWF, Panthera and the Smithsonian all repeat this, and camera-trap studies really do identify individuals by stripe pattern. But the absolute 'no two are the same' is an extrapolation from the tigers anyone has looked at — nobody has checked, or could check, every tiger. The checker refused to call the absolute wording verified.
facts.proposedRewrite: Every tiger has its own pattern of stripes. Scientists use them to tell tigers apart.

facts.fact: A hedgehog rolls up into a prickly ball when it feels worried.
facts.sourceNote: Wildlife Trusts: hedgehogs roll into a ball of spines when threatened. 'Worried' is the child-facing word for the same behaviour.

facts.fact: Squirrels bury nuts to eat later, and forget where some of them are.
facts.sourceNote: Squirrels do fail to recover a share of their caches each year. Researchers argue about whether that is true forgetting or deliberate abandonment of awkward caches, which does not change the fact as worded.

facts.fact: Mice have long whiskers that help them feel their way in the dark.
facts.sourceNote: Whiskers are touch-sensitive and especially useful to nocturnal animals such as mice navigating lightless burrows.

facts.fact: Moles dig tunnels with big front paws shaped like spades.
facts.sourceNote: Wildlife Trusts uses the phrase 'spade-like paws' for digging tunnels.

facts.fact: Badgers live underground in big tunnel homes called setts.
facts.sourceNote: Sussex Wildlife Trust: badgers live in family groups in a system of underground tunnels and chambers called a sett.

facts.fact: A baby frog is called a tadpole, and it swims like a little fish.
facts.sourceNote: NHM: tadpoles have gills and a tail they use to swim. No source uses the 'like a little fish' simile itself, but gilled-and-tail-propelled supports it as a comparison rather than a claim.

facts.fact: A toad has bumpy dry skin, and a frog has smooth damp skin.
facts.sourceNote: Woodland Trust: British toads have bumpy warty-looking skin that is virtually always dry; frogs have sleek smooth skin that usually looks wet.

facts.fact: A tortoise carries its hard shell everywhere, because the shell is part of its body.
facts.sourceNote: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance: the spine and ribs are fused to the carapace, so the shell cannot be left behind. Re-sourced off Wikipedia deliberately.

facts.fact: Newts live in ponds in spring and spend the rest of the year on land.
facts.sourceNote: Canal and River Trust: newts breed in spring in water and are terrestrial for the rest of the year. True of UK newts specifically.

facts.fact: A shrew is tiny and has to eat very often to keep its energy up.
facts.sourceNote: Mammal Society: common shrews have to eat every two to three hours to survive.

facts.fact: Dormice curl up and sleep right through the whole winter.
facts.sourceNote: Refuted on the word 'right through'. PTES itself notes dormice wake periodically during hibernation and even move nests, and the literature describes torpor bouts broken by arousals. They hibernate for months, but not continuously.
facts.proposedRewrite: Dormice curl up in a cosy nest and sleep for months all through the winter.

facts.fact: A vole looks like a mouse but has a rounder face and a shorter tail.
facts.sourceNote: Wildlife Trusts: voles have blunter, rounder faces, smaller ears and eyes, and shorter tails than mice.

facts.fact: A salamander can grow a new leg if it loses one.
facts.sourceNote: Smithsonian: a lost limb grows back at the right size and orientation. Best documented in the axolotl, which is a salamander.

facts.fact: Hamsters carry food in stretchy pouches inside their cheeks.
facts.sourceNote: Quotes Ed Spevak, curator at Saint Louis Zoo: stretchy cheek pouches that nearly triple in size, used to carry food back to the nest. Small caveat: the expert is a zoo curator but the outlet is a magazine — no UK vet charity page uses the word 'stretchy'.

facts.fact: Guinea pigs squeak and whistle to talk to each other.
facts.sourceNote: RSPCA Solent: wheeking is a high-pitched whistle, and chutting and rumbling are used socially between guinea pigs.

facts.fact: Gerbils come from dry sandy places and love to dig burrows.
facts.sourceNote: RSPCA: gerbils are burrowing rodents adapted to desert environments in Africa, India and Asia.

facts.fact: A pony is a horse that stays small even when it is fully grown.
facts.sourceNote: No UK equine authority (BHS, Blue Cross, World Horse Welfare, RSPCA) defines a pony this way, and the classification is not purely about size — Arabians are called horses however small, polo ponies are called ponies however tall. The 'not a baby horse' half is solidly right; the definition as a whole is not. Left flagged rather than reworded because the honest version is longer and less child-shaped, and that is Joe's call.
facts.proposedRewrite: A pony is not a baby horse. It is fully grown, and it stays small.

facts.fact: Ferrets do a happy hopping dance when they want to play.
facts.sourceNote: Woodgreen Pets Charity: excited, happy ferrets fluff their tails and jump around your feet, sometimes called the weasel dance. Re-sourced off Wikipedia.

facts.fact: Geckos have special toes that let them walk up walls.
facts.sourceNote: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Explorers: geckos crawl up house walls and across ceilings, using hairlike setae on the bottoms of their toes.

facts.fact: Chinchillas have very thick soft fur and take their baths in dust.
facts.sourceNote: PDSA: chinchillas need daily dust baths, not water, to keep their coats in condition. Fur density corroborated by Smithsonian National Zoo.

facts.fact: A terrapin is a small turtle that lives in fresh water.
facts.sourceNote: University of Kent (DICE) describes terrapins as freshwater turtles, which is the UK usage of the word. 'Small' is a fair simplification — pond terrapins run 18-20cm, though the RSPCA notes pet sliders can reach dinner-plate size.

facts.fact: Rats are very clever and can learn their way through a maze.
facts.sourceNote: PDSA: rats are very clever with very good memories, and once they learn a route they rarely forget it. Maze learning is one of the most replicated results in animal psychology.

facts.fact: Degus come from Chile and love to dig and play together.
facts.sourceNote: Animal Diversity Web: degus are endemic to Chile, burrow-digging, and highly social, living in groups with shared burrow systems.

facts.fact: Budgies come from Australia and fly in big flocks in the wild.
facts.sourceNote: BirdLife Australia: budgerigars are native to Australia and nomadic, with large flocks in open habitats, sometimes tens of thousands strong after rain.

facts.fact: Canaries are famous for their singing, and it is the males who sing most.
facts.sourceNote: Almost certainly true — male-biased song in canaries is textbook avian neuroscience — but flagged on sourcing, not on doubt. Two checkers could not reach an authoritative page: RSPCA, PDSA and Blue Cross publish no canary page (confirmed against their sitemaps), BirdLife's Island Canary factsheet carries no behaviour, and Birds of the World would not load. Only pet blogs say it. Cage birds sit in a gap between the vets and the zoos.

facts.fact: A cockatiel has a crest of feathers on its head that goes up and down.
facts.sourceNote: Same sourcing gap as the canary. Birds in Backyards describes the crest's look but not the raising and lowering; no zoo, museum, university or vet charity page could be reached that states the behaviour. Anyone who has met a cockatiel knows it, which is precisely why it went unchecked everywhere.

facts.fact: Lovebirds get their name because pairs like to sit close together.
facts.sourceNote: Same sourcing gap. The genus name Agapornis does mean 'love bird' in Greek and the close-perching is widely described, but only on commercial bird sites. Name-origin claims are exactly the sort that get repeated between blogs without anyone checking, so this one is flagged harder than the other two.

facts.fact: Many bears sleep in a cosy den all winter and wake up in spring.
facts.sourceNote: Alaska Fish and Game: bears den for months without eating or drinking. Caveat the checker raised and did not think fatal: this is torpor rather than true hibernation, and bears do stir inside the den. 'Many' also covers bears that do not den at all.

facts.fact: Otters have thick fur that keeps them warm and dry in the water.
facts.sourceNote: US National Park Service: the waterproofing of the outer layers of fur keeps the skin dry and warm all year.

facts.fact: Chipmunks stuff their cheeks full of seeds to carry them home.
facts.sourceNote: Forest Preserve District: chipmunks fill their cheek pouches with seeds and nuts and carry them to pantry chambers in the burrow.

facts.fact: Elk grow huge antlers, and lose them and grow new ones every year.
facts.sourceNote: Refuted as worded. Only bull elk grow antlers; cows normally do not, and the rare exceptions are hormonal abnormalities. Saying 'elk grow huge antlers' is wrong for half the species.
facts.proposedRewrite: Male elk grow huge antlers. They drop them and grow new ones every year.

facts.fact: Pine martens are brilliant climbers and live high up in the trees.
facts.sourceNote: Refuted on the second half. Woodland Trust confirms they are superb climbers, but also says pine martens find most of their food on the ground. They are semi-arboreal — they den and rest up high — so 'live high up in the trees' overstates it.
facts.proposedRewrite: Pine martens are brilliant climbers. They rest and sleep high up in hollow trees.

facts.fact: A stoat's brown coat can turn white in winter to match the snow.
facts.sourceNote: Mammal Society: stoats in colder and more northern parts of the UK can turn white in winter (ermine). Southern English stoats usually stay brown, which is why the fact says 'can'.

facts.fact: A lynx has furry black tufts on the tips of its ears.
facts.sourceNote: San Diego Zoo: the lynx is known by the tuft of black hair on the tips of its ears.

facts.fact: A skunk can make a very smelly spray to keep others away.
facts.sourceNote: National Geographic Kids: skunks spray a noxious-smelling liquid from glands near the tail as a defence.

facts.fact: A porcupine's coat is covered in sharp spines called quills.
facts.sourceNote: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance: porcupines are wrapped in a coat of more than 30,000 sharp quills.

facts.fact: A wolverine's thick furry coat stops snow and frost sticking to it.
facts.sourceNote: Actively refuted. Testing reported by researcher Boris Pavlin found wolverine fur is NOT hydrophobic and frost does form on it. The real property is that the frost brushes off easily rather than freezing hard. The drafted fact says the opposite of what the evidence shows.
facts.proposedRewrite: A wolverine's thick coat lets frost brush straight off instead of freezing hard.

facts.fact: Hares have longer ears and longer legs than rabbits, and they run very fast.
facts.sourceNote: Wildlife Trusts: the brown hare is larger than the rabbit with longer legs and longer ears, and is the fastest UK land mammal.

facts.fact: The Scottish wildcat looks like a pet cat but has a thick stripy tail.
facts.sourceNote: Woodland Trust: resembles a large tabby but has a distinctive thick bushy tail with black rings and a blunt black tip.

facts.fact: Minks are strong swimmers and their thick fur keeps the water out.
facts.sourceNote: Iowa DNR: mink are strong swimmers with partially webbed feet, and their fur is waterproofed by oily guard hairs.

facts.fact: A coypu is a big furry animal that swims in rivers, and it has orange teeth.
facts.sourceNote: Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency: the coypu is a large semi-aquatic rodent of rivers and marshes with distinctive dark-orange incisors.

facts.fact: Male pheasants have bright feathers and a very long tail.
facts.sourceNote: RSPB: large, long-tailed game birds; the male has rich chestnut, golden-brown and black markings with a dark green head and red face wattling.

facts.fact: The capercaillie is a huge woodland bird that lives in Scottish pine forests.
facts.sourceNote: RSPB: a huge woodland grouse, the males large and unmistakable, breeding in Scottish native pinewood. Its conservation status was deliberately left out of the fact — S19 bars frightening framing.

facts.fact: Every zebra has its very own pattern of stripes.
facts.sourceNote: San Diego Zoo states it plainly: each zebra has a unique stripe pattern, and researchers use it to identify individuals. Note this fact avoids the absolute 'no two are ever alike' that got the tiger row flagged.

facts.fact: Hippos spend the hot part of the day in the water to stay cool.
facts.sourceNote: African Wildlife Foundation: hippos rely on water or mud to keep cool, spending up to 16 hours a day submerged in daylight.

facts.fact: The cheetah is the fastest runner of all the land animals.
facts.sourceNote: Smithsonian National Zoo: the cheetah is the world's fastest land mammal. The fact gives no number, since published top speeds vary between sources.

facts.fact: One meerkat stands up tall to keep watch while the others are busy.
facts.sourceNote: National Geographic: one or more meerkats act as sentries on a high point, often on their hind legs, while the rest of the group forages.

facts.fact: A warthog kneels down on its front knees to eat short grass.
facts.sourceNote: Maryland Zoo: the warthog kneels on thick calloused knees to graze short grass more easily.

facts.fact: Gorillas make a new leafy nest to sleep in every night.
facts.sourceNote: Smithsonian National Zoo: before dusk each gorilla over about three years old builds its own fresh nest.

facts.fact: Antelopes have horns that stay on for life, unlike a deer's antlers.
facts.sourceNote: US National Park Service: horns are permanent, antlers are shed and regrown yearly. Caveat: the pronghorn sheds its horn sheath annually, but the pronghorn is not a true antelope, so the claim holds for the group as meant.

facts.fact: Some mongooses live together in big family groups and take turns keeping watch.
facts.sourceNote: African Wildlife Foundation: dwarf mongooses live in family groups of 12-15 and swap guard duty through the day so each can forage. True of dwarf and banded species, not all mongooses — hence 'some'.

facts.fact: Hyenas make a funny whooping sound that people say is like a laugh.
facts.sourceNote: Refuted as worded: the fact conflates two different calls. The whoop is a long-distance contact call; the separate giggle is the one people call a laugh. Note for Joe: the giggle is a stress call, made when an animal is harassed or frustrated, so the softer 'laugh' framing is a bit of a fiction either way.
facts.proposedRewrite: Hyenas make a giggling sound that people say is like a laugh.

facts.fact: Baboons live in big troops and groom each other's fur to stay friendly.
facts.sourceNote: San Diego Zoo: baboon troops use social grooming to reinforce bonds within the group.

facts.fact: Huge herds of wildebeest walk a very long way each year to find fresh grass.
facts.sourceNote: African Wildlife Foundation: wildebeest migrate in a circle of 800-1,610 km a year, following the rains and fresh grass.

facts.fact: African buffalo stay together in big herds and like to wallow in mud.
facts.sourceNote: African Wildlife Foundation: herds of hundreds, sometimes joining into thousands, and regular mud wallowing for cooling and pests.

facts.fact: An aardvark has a long sticky tongue and digs with very strong claws.
facts.sourceNote: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance: a long sticky tongue for termites and ants, and strong front legs with long claws for digging burrows.

facts.fact: A sheep's woolly coat is cut off each summer, and then it grows back.
facts.sourceNote: British Wool: the welfare code requires mature sheep be shorn at least once a year and the fleece regrows continuously. 'Each summer' is a fair simplification of 'at least yearly, in the warm months'.

facts.fact: Goats are brilliant climbers and can balance on very steep rocks.
facts.sourceNote: US National Park Service: mountain goats climb slopes over 60 degrees using cloven hooves that grip. Caveat: the extreme version is the wild mountain goat; farm goats are good climbers but less spectacular.

facts.fact: Horses can sleep standing up as well as lying down.
facts.sourceNote: Horses doze standing, locked upright by the stay apparatus, but must lie down for REM sleep. The fact says 'as well as lying down' for exactly that reason.

facts.fact: Donkeys have much longer ears than horses, and a loud hee-haw call.
facts.sourceNote: Donkeys have notably larger ears than horses, an adaptation for losing heat, and bray rather than whinny.

facts.fact: Geese fly in a V shape to help each other on long journeys.
facts.sourceNote: WWT: the V gives following birds aerodynamic lift and saves energy, and the lead position is rotated so no one goose tires out.

facts.fact: A turkey's head can change colour when it gets excited.
facts.sourceNote: National Wild Turkey Federation: the head and snood change colour, shifting between red, white and blue, when the bird is excited or agitated.

facts.fact: Llamas carry bags for people, and they hum softly to each other.
facts.sourceNote: Denver Zoo: llamas carry loads up to 130lb as pack animals, and mothers hum to their young, who hum back. Re-sourced off an aggregator site; note the extension services describe the pack use but not the humming, so the humming rests on the zoo alone.

facts.fact: Alpacas are smaller than llamas and are kept for their soft fleece.
facts.sourceNote: Rutgers Cooperative Extension: llamas are roughly twice the size of alpacas, and alpacas are raised chiefly for their fine soft fibre.

facts.fact: A rooster crows in the morning, and often at other times too.
facts.sourceNote: Nagoya University (Shimmura and Yoshimura): crowing runs off an internal circadian clock anticipating dawn, but roosters also crow at light and noise through the day. The second clause is deliberate — 'roosters crow only at dawn' is the myth this fact is written against.

facts.fact: An ox is a cow trained to pull heavy carts and ploughs.
facts.sourceNote: Refuted on 'a cow'. An ox is a castrated adult male bovine trained for draught work; 'cow' means an adult female. The training half is right, the sex is wrong, and it would teach her something she would later have to unlearn.
facts.proposedRewrite: An ox is a big strong bull trained to pull heavy carts and ploughs.

facts.fact: A mule has a horse for a mum and a donkey for a dad.
facts.sourceNote: A mule is a male donkey crossed with a female horse. The checker was told to watch the direction specifically, because the reverse cross is a hinny — the fact has it the right way round.

facts.fact: Chickens talk to each other with lots of different clucks and calls.
facts.sourceNote: University of Maryland Extension lists many distinct chicken vocalisations — food calls, cackles, purring, tidbitting and more.

facts.fact: Guinea fowl have spotty feathers and make a very loud noise.
facts.sourceNote: Half sourced, half not. University of Kentucky poultry extension is emphatic about the noise. No extension, zoo or museum page reached actually describes the plumage as spotted — they name the 'pearl' variety without describing it. Flagged rather than trimmed, because the spots are the thing a child would recognise.
facts.proposedRewrite: Guinea fowl are farmyard birds that make a very loud noise indeed.

facts.fact: Quails are small round birds that would rather run than fly.
facts.sourceNote: Cornell Lab uses almost this wording — Gambel's Quail 'would rather run than fly' — and describes them as small, round, ground-dwelling birds. Re-sourced off a commercial bird site.

facts.fact: Water buffalo love to wallow in muddy water to stay cool.
facts.sourceNote: Water buffalo have far fewer sweat glands than cattle and wallow for up to five hours a day in the heat to cool down.

facts.fact: Pigeons can find their way home from far away places.
facts.sourceNote: Smithsonian: homing is well documented, using magnetic sensing, sun position and landmarks. The fact claims the ability, not the mechanism, which is still argued over.
